title: The partly column
hook: modern writers, not Epictetus, add a third column: things partly up to me

segments.voice: Yesterday: the archer, who does everything to aim well and lets the wind have the rest. Your line was aim, then let go. What did you aim at, and did you let it go? Day one hundred thirteen.

Try Epictetus's two columns on a real worry, and something awkward happens. Say you're worried about your health. Is that up to you? Not entirely. Genes, accidents, luck. Not up to you at all? That doesn't feel right either: you choose what you eat, whether you walk, whether you see a doctor. Or your kid's grades. Your marriage. Your job. Plenty of the things people actually lie awake about don't fit neatly in either column. They sit somewhere in between. Modern writers noticed this, and some of them drew a third column. Today: the partly column.
screen: `YOUR HEALTH: MINE?` → `NOT ENTIRELY. NOT NOT.` → `A THIRD COLUMN.`

segments.voice: First, the honest history. Epictetus had two columns, not three. The third was added in our own time, notably by the American philosophy professor William Irvine in a 2009 book on Stoic practice, where he called it the trichotomy of control: things we have complete control over, things we have no control over, and things we have some control over. Some Stoic scholars push back. They say Epictetus didn't need a third column, because anything partly up to you can be split into the part that's yours and the part that isn't. And here's the useful thing: if you follow either path carefully, you end up in the same place. Take the tennis match, Irvine's own example. Winning is partly up to you. You can't control your opponent, the wind or the line judge. So what do you do with the partly column? You break it open, and look for the piece that is fully yours: to practice hard, to play as well as you can today. That becomes your goal. Not win, but play my best. Which is exactly Cato's archer from yesterday, aiming well and letting the result go. The partly column isn't a place to leave things. It's a place to open things up. Your health: the walk, the vegetables, the appointment are yours; the rest is not. Your kid's grades: the quiet desk, the encouragement, the patience are yours; the grades are theirs. Find your part. Do your part. Let the rest be the rest.
screen: `EPICTETUS HAD TWO COLUMNS.` · `IRVINE, 2009: A THIRD.` · `BREAK IT OPEN.` · `FIND THE PIECE THAT'S FULLY YOURS.` · then, large: `MY PART ONLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one partly-mine thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you care about that's partly up to you. Your health, a relationship, a project. Hold it in mind. Now break it open. Ask: what, in this, is fully mine? Maybe one call, one habit, one kind word, one hour. Name it clearly. Then set the rest down beside it, gently: not mine. Breathe with your part in your hands. The bell holds the time.
Trichotomy. William Irvine's name for the third column, what's partly up to you, broken open to find the piece that's fully yours. Today's word.
Your line: my part only. Today, when something big and tangled weighs on you, ask: what's my part? Do that part well, and let the rest be the rest. Day one hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Some modern readers of Stoicism use a three-column sort, following William Irvine: what's fully up to me, what isn't, and what's partly up to me, which they break down until they find the piece that is fully theirs.

fork.reveal: winning is only partly yours. playing your best is fully yours, so that becomes the goal. it's the archer again.
